chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Term Structure of Volatility

lessons.title: Reading India VIX Futures Term Structure

children.text: A Different Curve: Futures on the Fear Gauge Itself

Chapter 1 defined India VIX as NSE's own aggregate implied volatility number, computed from the live Nifty options order book, representing the market's 30-calendar-day expected volatility. VIX futures are a genuinely separate instrument: a futures contract that settles based on where India VIX itself will actually sit on some future date. Plot the futures price of each available contract against its expiry, and you get a curve that looks similar to the term structures earlier in this chapter, but is built from a completely different underlying instrument.

body.text: Do not conflate the two curves this chapter has now covered. The Nifty option ATM IV term structure (Lessons 1 to 3) is built from actual Nifty option prices, across Nifty's own expiries. The VIX futures term structure is built from futures contracts on India VIX itself, a separate, one-level-removed instrument. They rhyme for similar underlying reasons, but they are not the same object.

children.text: Why VIX Futures Usually Sit in Contango Too

Lesson 2 explained Nifty option IV's usual contango shape through volatility mean reversion: calm current conditions expected to drift back up toward a higher long-run average. The exact same logic applies directly to VIX futures, one level more literally. India VIX itself spends most of its time in a low, calm range and tends to revert toward a higher long-run average over time, so a futures contract on India VIX, expiring a month or two from now, typically prices somewhat above today's spot VIX reading. The result is a curve that usually slopes gently upward, the same contango shape, now applied to the futures price of the fear gauge itself rather than to Nifty option IV.

body.caption: Illustrative India VIX futures curve, calm market conditions

children.text: When It Inverts: VIX Futures Backwardation as a Stress Signal

During genuine market stress, this curve can flip hard. Spot VIX spikes to a level the market does not expect to persist, so near-month futures trade below spot, and the curve inverts into backwardation. This is an extremely well-documented pattern on the globally liquid CBOE VIX futures market, most famously during the March 2020 COVID crash and the 2008 financial crisis, when spot VIX shot far above where futures a few months out were still pricing, because traders expected the acute panic to fade well before those later contracts settled.
Why This Matters Even If You Never Trade a VIX Future: Roll Yield

VIX futures expire and have to be replaced to maintain ongoing exposure. Any fund or product trying to hold constant volatility exposure has to continually roll out of the expiring near-month contract and into the next one. When the curve sits in contango, its normal resting state, that roll is structurally costly: selling the cheaper, expiring contract and buying the pricier further-out one, month after month. This persistent drag, called negative roll yield, is the well-documented reason globally traded "long volatility" products have tended to bleed value steadily over long periods, even though the underlying volatility index they track genuinely does spike, sometimes dramatically, during individual crises along the way.

body.text: A product that promises exposure to "rising volatility" is not automatically a good long-term hedge. If it maintains that exposure by rolling futures through a persistently contangoed curve, it can lose value steadily for months at a time, and still not fully make that back even during a real spike, unless the spike is large enough and the timing lucky enough to outrun the accumulated roll cost.

children.text: Everything above describes a well-established global framework, built on the deeply liquid CBOE VIX futures market. India VIX futures exist on NSE, but have historically traded with far thinner volume and open interest than Nifty or Bank Nifty derivatives, and their liquidity has fluctuated significantly over the years. Before assuming this is a readily tradeable instrument on any given day, verify its current listing status, volume, and open interest directly on NSE. Partly because of this gap, many Indian desks watch the shape of the more liquid global VIX futures curves alongside India VIX itself, as a broader cross-market read on sentiment, rather than relying solely on India's own VIX futures.

body.title: Telling the two curves apart
body.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes India VIX futures term structure from the Nifty option ATM IV term structure covered earlier in this chapter?
options: They are the same curve, just described using two different names

The Nifty option term structure plots the ATM implied volatility of Nifty options across different expiries; the VIX futures term structure plots the market's futures price for where India VIX itself will be at different future dates, a related but genuinely distinct instrument
VIX futures term structure only exists during an actual market crash
Nifty option IV term structure is mathematically derived directly from VIX futures prices
body.explanation: The two curves rhyme because they are both shaped by volatility mean reversion and event risk, but they are built from different instruments: one from Nifty options directly, the other from futures contracts on the VIX index itself, a separate, one-level-removed product.

body.title: Why the 'long volatility' fund lost money despite real VIX spikes
body.scenario: An investor bought units of a hypothetical "long India volatility" fund two years ago, expecting it to rise sharply whenever markets turn turbulent. Over the two years, India VIX itself spiked sharply on three separate occasions, each time by 60% or more, yet the fund's overall value is down almost 40% over the same period.
body.prompt: Using what you know about VIX futures term structure, explain the most likely reason for this outcome, even though VIX itself clearly spiked multiple times.
body.modelAnswer: The fund most likely maintains its exposure by continually rolling VIX futures contracts as they expire. Since the curve sits in contango most of the time, its normal resting state, each roll systematically sells a cheaper, expiring near-month contract and buys a pricier further-out one, a structural drag that compounds month after month during every calm stretch. The three genuine VIX spikes produced real, sharp gains when they happened, but brief spikes are usually not large or frequent enough to outweigh the steady contango-driven bleed accumulated across all the calm months in between. This is exactly the well-documented pattern seen in globally traded long-volatility products: real crisis-day payoffs, offset by a much longer, quieter cost of simply holding the position while waiting for them.

body.title: Nifty Option IV Term Structure vs VIX Futures Term Structure

columns.label: Nifty Option ATM IV Term Structure
points: Plots the implied volatility backed out of actual Nifty option prices, across expiries
Directly tradeable through the options themselves
Covered in Lessons 1 through 3 of this chapter
Reflects hedging demand and event risk specific to Nifty

columns.label: India VIX Futures Term Structure
points: Plots the futures price for India VIX itself, across future dates
A separate, distinct instrument; liquidity has historically been much thinner than Nifty or Bank Nifty derivatives in India specifically
Usually sits in contango in calm markets, inverts into backwardation during acute stress, for the same underlying reasons
Its shape drives roll yield: the structural cost, or occasionally benefit, of continuously holding rolled volatility futures exposure

body.text: VIX futures do for the fear gauge itself what Nifty options do for the index: they price not just today's fear, but tomorrow's expected fear, across an entire calendar of future dates. Reading that curve, and understanding why holding it usually costs money in calm markets, is the difference between using volatility as a genuine hedge and slowly bleeding value while waiting for a crisis that might not arrive on schedule.

points: India VIX futures term structure plots the market's futures price for India VIX itself across future dates, a distinct instrument from the Nifty option ATM IV term structure covered earlier in this chapter.
VIX futures usually sit in contango in calm markets, for the same mean-reversion logic as Lesson 2: VIX itself tends to revert toward a higher long-run average over time.

VIX futures term structure inverts into backwardation during acute market stress, a well-documented global pattern, since spot VIX spikes far above what the market still expects it to be a few months out.

Roll yield is the structural cost, in contango, or benefit, in backwardation, of continuously rolling VIX futures exposure; persistent contango is the well-documented reason long-volatility products have often bled value over time despite real spikes along the way.

India VIX futures have historically traded with much thinner liquidity than Nifty and Bank Nifty derivatives; always verify current listing status, volume, and open interest on NSE before assuming this is a readily tradeable instrument.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The VIX futures curve table and the long-volatility fund scenario are hypothetical and illustrative. India VIX futures' liquidity has varied significantly over time and may be limited or thin; always verify current listing status, volume, and open interest directly on NSE before assuming this or any derivative product is readily tradeable. Always check live prices on NSE or your broker's terminal before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
